paragraphs: Cassius Clay was a 7-to-1 underdog against Sonny Liston in Miami Beach on 25 February 1964, and reporters worried openly he might be hurt badly. Liston, a feared ex-convict who had destroyed Floyd Patterson twice in the first round, quit on his stool before the seventh round with a shoulder injury, having been unable to land a solid punch on the faster, taller Clay. Clay screamed at ringside press to eat their words.

Days later he announced he had joined the Nation of Islam and would be known as Muhammad Ali, a name most sportswriters refused to use for years afterward. The rematch, in Lewiston, Maine in 1965, ended in the first round on a punch many at ringside said they never saw land, feeding lasting doubts about whether it was a real knockout.

DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 games to 1 in Seoul in March 2016. Go has far more possible positions than chess, so programmers had long assumed it would resist brute-force computation for decades; AlphaGo instead used neural networks trained on human games and then on games played against itself.

Lee's single win, in game four, came after he found an unusual move that AlphaGo's own commentators said its programmers had not anticipated, and it remains the last game a human has won against a top Go program. Lee retired from professional play in 2019, saying an AI opponent that could not be beaten had made the pursuit feel different to him.

Queen Anne spotted a stretch of open heathland near Windsor Castle while out riding and judged it ideal for horses to gallop at full stretch. She had a course laid out on Ascot Heath, and the first meeting ran there on 11 August 1711: seven horses competed for Her Majesty's Plate, a purse of 100 guineas decided across three separate four mile heats.

Ascot's royal connection has held ever since. The monarch still processes down the course by carriage each year during Royal Ascot week, a tradition begun under George IV in the 1820s. What started as one queen's afternoon experiment with a patch of open ground grew into one of the fixed points of the British racing and social calendar.

Babe Ruth had set the single-season home run record four times already before 1927, each time breaking his own mark. Playing for a Yankees lineup so dominant it was nicknamed Murderers' Row, he hit his 60th on the second-to-last day of the season, off Washington's Tom Zachary.

The total exceeded what all but one other team in the American League hit that year, and was the record for 34 seasons until Roger Maris hit 61 in 1961, in a longer schedule that prompted talk of an asterisk. Ruth's 1927 mark had itself once seemed unapproachable.

Roger Bannister ran a mile in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds at Oxford's Iffley Road track on 6 May 1954, using two friends as pacemakers, Chris Chataway and Chris Brasher. He was a 25-year-old medical student who trained on his lunch break, since the meeting had no professional runners then. The announcer only got as far as three minutes before the crowd's roar drowned out the rest of the time.

The record lasted 46 days before Australian John Landy ran it faster in Turku, Finland, and the two met weeks later in Vancouver in a race billed as the Mile of the Century, which Bannister won. He retired from competitive running soon after to finish his medical training and became a neurologist. The four-minute barrier had been treated as a physiological limit for decades before it fell.

James Naismith was a physical education instructor at a Massachusetts YMCA training school, told to invent an indoor game to occupy restless students through the New England winter. He nailed two peach baskets to the gymnasium balcony rails and wrote thirteen rules, including a ban on running with the ball, in December 1891.

The baskets kept their bottoms for years, so someone had to fetch a ladder to retrieve the ball after every score until an open-ended net replaced them. Naismith's original class of eighteen played the first game nine against nine, with a soccer ball, on a court smaller than a modern half-court.

Billie Jean King beat 55-year-old Bobby Riggs in straight sets, 6-4, 6-3, 6-3, before roughly 30,000 spectators at the Houston Astrodome on 20 September 1973, in a match broadcast to an estimated 90 million viewers worldwide. Riggs, a former world number one decades earlier, had already beaten Margaret Court in a match earlier that year and goaded King into accepting the rematch with a stream of publicity stunts.

King was carried into the arena on a feather-adorned litter borne by four men, a deliberate mockery of Riggs's own entrance on a rickshaw pulled by models. She had pushed for equal prize money at the US Open the year before and threatened a boycott to get it. The match is credited with boosting participation and sponsorship in women's tennis at a moment when equal pay for female athletes was barely discussed.

Constantinople's Hippodrome held roughly 100,000 spectators watching chariots race around a central spine decorated with looted obelisks and bronze statues. Support split along two chariot factions, the Blues and the Greens, whose rivalry ran well beyond sport into politics, religion and street violence, since emperors courted both for popular backing.

That rivalry exploded in January 532, when a joint protest by both factions over harsh sentences for rioters turned into the Nika riots. Crowds tried to crown a new emperor, and Justinian's general Belisarius put down the revolt by trapping the mob inside the Hippodrome itself, where a massacre reported at around 30,000 dead ended the uprising.

In 1756 the London mathematician William Payne published the first English language treatise on draughts, with its dedication and preface written by Samuel Johnson. Before Payne's book, jumping and crowning rules varied enough from town to town that a game could be played to completely different endings depending on where it was played.

Payne's treatise fixed rules still recognisable today, including the huff, which let a player remove an opponent's piece for failing to take a forced jump, and a strict touch move convention. The game itself is older, its diagonal capturing moves descended from a piece added to chess variants centuries earlier, but Payne's book is what gave English draughts, called checkers in America, one agreed rulebook.

Chaturanga is first described clearly in the Harshacharita, written by the poet Banabhatta around 625 CE for the court of Emperor Harsha, though the game itself is generally placed a little earlier, in Gupta era India around the sixth century. The name comes from Sanskrit for four limbs, the four arms of an army it modelled: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

Trade carried it into Persia as shatranj, where the Sanskrit rajah became the Persian shah, the word English speakers eventually mangled into check and checkmate. Centuries of onward travel through the Islamic world and into Europe reshaped the pieces and the rules almost beyond recognition, but the board of four contending arms is still there under the modern queen, bishop and knight.

Chariots had already been racing in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills for centuries by 329 BCE. What that year actually marks is narrower: the building of the first permanent starting gates, replacing whatever temporary barriers had served before and letting races start several chariots at once on genuinely equal footing.

Seven wooden eggs sat on the central spina to mark laps, removed one by one as the race wore on, an addition that only arrived later, in 174 BCE. The track kept racing for the best part of a thousand years after those first stone gates, with the last recorded chariot race there run in 549 CE.

Arthur Wynne, a British-born editor putting together the Christmas puzzle page for the New York World, needed something new for readers bored of the usual word squares. In December 1913 he printed a diamond-shaped grid with a hollow centre and called it a Word-Cross, giving clues numbered to blank cells rather than a filled pattern.

A typesetting error a few weeks later swapped the name to Cross-Word, and the hyphen soon dropped. Wynne kept producing them for the World, which had no idea it had started a craze; other papers were slow to pick the format up, and the crossword did not become a fixture of American newspapers until the 1920s.

Cuju began as infantry drill during the Warring States period, soldiers kicking a feather stuffed leather ball to sharpen agility and footwork well before it was anyone's game. By the Han dynasty it had left the barracks: the dynasty's first emperor had a cuju court built at his own palace around 206 BCE, and a military manual from the period is the earliest documentary evidence FIFA recognises for any kicking game.

Han rules already barred using the hands, the same basic restriction football keeps today, though cuju was played toward a small goal rather than across an open pitch. It stayed popular through several dynasties before an outright ban under the Ming, whose first emperor judged it a distraction from proper soldiering rather than useful training for it.

IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 over a six-game match in New York in May 1997, after Kasparov had won a shorter match against an earlier version of the machine the previous year. Kasparov resigned game six after just 19 moves, a collapse he later attributed to psychological pressure rather than a purely technical loss.

Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, suspecting a human grandmaster had intervened during a puzzling move in game two, and demanded the printouts of the machine's calculations. IBM refused and dismantled Deep Blue soon after rather than agree to a rematch. The match is still cited as the moment computers were accepted as capable of beating the best humans at a task long treated as a marker of pure intellect.

Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson published Dungeons & Dragons in 1974 through Gygax's small company Tactical Studies Rules. It grew out of Chainmail, a medieval miniatures wargame Gygax had co-written, after Arneson began running a fantasy campaign focused on one hero exploring a dungeon rather than armies fighting battles. The rulebooks were typewritten and stapled, sold mostly by mail.

The game introduced the idea of a referee, the Dungeon Master, narrating an open-ended story rather than a fixed set of moves, which had no real precedent in commercial games. Gygax and Arneson later fell out over royalties and credit, and Arneson sued the company twice before settling. The genre it founded fed directly into early computer role-playing and dungeon-crawl video games.

The rock cut tombs at Beni Hasan, painted around 2000 BCE, carry hundreds of paired figures locked in throws, pins and counters along a single wall. Tomb 15, built for the local governor Baqet III, alone shows well over a hundred pairs in sequence, close enough in stance that later wrestlers can still recognise the holds.

Nothing this detailed survives from anywhere else in the ancient world, which makes Beni Hasan the oldest instruction manual for a sport that exists, even though no accompanying text names a single move. The painters were not illustrating a contest so much as cataloguing technique, pair after pair, for a governor who evidently wanted his wrestlers remembered.

Eleven London and suburban clubs met at the Freemasons Tavern in October 1863 to agree a single set of rules for football, ending years of each school and club playing its own variant. The Football Association's laws banned running with the ball in hand and hacking an opponent's shins, the two features that made rugby football recognisably distinct.

The split with rugby was not immediate. Blackheath, one of the founding clubs, walked out when hacking was outlawed and never affiliated with the FA, and rugby did not organise its own governing body until 1871. The FA's 1863 laws nonetheless became the template followed by association football clubs across Britain and beyond.

A Dutchman working in Paris, Robert Guerin, pushed for an international body after growing frustrated that the English Football Association showed little interest in governing the game beyond Britain. Seven national associations, France, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland, founded FIFA in Paris in May 1904.

England's FA, invited but unconvinced an international federation was needed, joined only the following year. FIFA's early decades were run on a shoestring by volunteers coordinating fixtures between a handful of European associations, a far cry from the global tournament body it later became.

Alexander Cartwright is often credited as baseball's inventor, but the rules the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club adopted on 23 September 1845 were drawn up by a club committee that included William Wheaton, who had already written similar rules for New York's Gotham Club. What Cartwright did was insist the Knickerbockers play by no other version, helping one set of rules spread rather than compete with a dozen local variants.

Those twenty rules fixed the diamond shaped infield, foul territory, and the practice of tagging or throwing to a base rather than hitting a runner with the ball, which had been standard in the rounders like games baseball grew out of. The story that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown is a later fabrication with no supporting evidence.

Inspired by the marathon revived at the 1896 Athens Olympics, members of the Boston Athletic Association organised their own race for Patriots' Day in April 1897. Fifteen runners started from Metcalf's Mill in Ashland and ran roughly 24.5 miles to Boston, a distance not yet standardised at today's 26.2 miles.

John J. McDermott of New York won in a little under three hours, walking part of an uphill stretch before recovering to finish first. Ten men completed the course. The race has run every year since, surviving both World Wars, and is the oldest continuously held annual marathon in the world.

On 24 April 1741, Broughton fought George Stevenson at his amphitheatre off Oxford Road, then on London's edge. Stevenson went down repeatedly over four rounds and died of his injuries a few days later; the rules Broughton wrote two years afterward, dated 16 August 1743, opened by outlawing exactly what had killed him.

Those seven rules gave a fallen fighter thirty seconds to rise unassisted, but matches stayed bare-knuckle. Broughton padded a fighter's fists only later, in February 1747, with leather 'mufflers' stuffed with horsehair, and only for sparring at the separate academy where he taught gentlemen who did not want to be bloodied.

The first Derby ran at Epsom Downs on 4 May 1780 over a mile, open to three year old colts and fillies at 50 guineas a stake. Diomed, owned by Sir Charles Bunbury and ridden by Sam Arnull, won the nine runner field as favourite, a result later obscured by the story that the race's name was settled by a coin toss between Bunbury and the twelfth Earl of Derby.

Whichever account of the naming is true, the earl's title stuck, and the word derby went on to mean any major sporting showpiece, from football to cricket. The distance was lengthened to a mile and a half within a few years, and that longer trip has stayed the Derby's defining test of a middle distance thoroughbred ever since.

Carl Fisher had built the Indianapolis Motor Speedway in 1909 as a testing ground for the local car industry, but its brick surface killed spectators and drivers alike at shorter races. To draw a bigger crowd worth the risk, organisers staged one long race a year instead of many short ones: 500 miles, over 200 laps, on Memorial Day 1911.

Ray Harroun drove a car of his own design, the Marmon Wasp, fitted with a rear-view mirror because he raced without a riding mechanic to watch for traffic, a first for American racing. He won at an average speed of about 74 miles per hour, and the brick track soon earned the nickname the Brickyard.

John Spilsbury, a London mapmaker and engraver, pasted one of his own maps onto a thin sheet of mahogany and cut along the borders of each country, producing a puzzle meant to teach children geography rather than to entertain. His 1766 dissected map of Europe divided into its kingdoms is the earliest surviving example of the form.

Spilsbury went on to cut puzzles of the other continents, England and Wales, Ireland and Scotland, advertising himself as an engraver and map dissector in wood. The radial cut of the mahogany he used let the wood expand and contract evenly, which is part of why some of his original puzzles still survive intact, over two and a half centuries on.

Meriwether Lewis Clark Jr, grandson of the explorer William Clark, had toured English and French racecourses and returned to Louisville determined to build something similar. He organised the Louisville Jockey Club, laid out Churchill Downs on land borrowed from relatives, and staged the first Derby on 17 May 1875 before a crowd estimated at ten thousand.

A colt named Aristides, ridden by a Black jockey, Oliver Lewis, won the mile-and-a-half race. Black riders dominated the Derby's early decades, taking fifteen of the first twenty-eight runnings, before Jim Crow-era exclusion pushed them out of the sport almost entirely by the 1920s.

The story that pupil William Webb Ellis invented rugby in 1823 by picking up the ball and running with it first appeared decades later, in a letter written by a schoolmate; running with the ball was against the rules at the time. In 1845 a committee of Rugby School pupils wrote down the Laws of Football as Played at Rugby School, the first published rules for any code of football.

That written code did not mention Webb Ellis at all; his name was attached to the sport only after his death, once old boys wanted an origin story. The 1845 rules nonetheless fixed what already set Rugby's version apart from other schools' football, handling and running with the ball, and other clubs adopting those laws is what actually gave the sport its name.

The earliest clear reference to cricket comes not from a scorecard but from a Sussex church court. In 1611, Bartholomew Wyatt and Richard Latter of Sidlesham were fined and ordered to do penance for skipping Easter Sunday service to play cricket instead, proof the game already had enough of a following to draw men away from church.

That the record survives at all is thanks to those ecclesiastical courts, which policed Sunday observance and left the paperwork historians now mine for early sport. Cricket had clearly existed earlier as an informal pastime among Weald villagers in Kent and Sussex, but nothing written down proves it before this prosecution, so the game's true origin is simply undated.

In 264 BCE, the sons of the Roman noble Decimus Junius Brutus Pera staged three pairs of slaves to fight to the death at his funeral, in the city's cattle market rather than any arena built for the purpose. It was framed as a munus, a duty owed to a dead ancestor, replacing an older custom of simply killing captives at a warrior's grave.

That handful of fights at one funeral is the acknowledged start of a practice that Roman aristocrats kept expanding for its political value, staging ever larger combats to win public favour long before the state built permanent amphitheatres for it. What began as private mourning became, within a couple of centuries, entertainment organised and paid for by the government itself.

Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, never saw the trophy he donated in action. He bought a plain silver bowl in England for about ten pounds, intended it as a challenge cup for the country's best amateur hockey club, and sailed home to Britain before it was first awarded in 1893.

The Montreal Hockey Club claimed it as champions of the Amateur Hockey Association of Canada, with no playoff game required that first year. The trophy later passed through amateur challenge matches before becoming, in the twentieth century, the championship of professional hockey's National Hockey League.

The Rome 1960 Games drew about 400 athletes from 23 countries, all competing in wheelchairs, and were originally billed as the 9th International Stoke Mandeville Games rather than as an Olympic event. Only spinal cord injuries were eligible; the broader disability categories used today came later. Rome had agreed to host after the city's own Olympics closed weeks earlier, using some of the same venues.

The Games trace back to Ludwig Guttmann, a neurologist who had organised wheelchair archery for injured war veterans at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England in 1948, the same week as the London Olympics. He saw competitive sport as rehabilitation rather than charity, and pushed to move the event onto an international, then Olympic, stage. Rome 1960 was retroactively recognised as the first Paralympic Games.

An England touring side, mostly amateurs on a private cricketing tour of Australia and New Zealand, played a match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in March 1877 that nobody at the time labelled a Test. The term was applied retrospectively; the players saw it as one fixture among many on a long, exhausting tour.

Australia won by 45 runs, a margin repeated almost exactly a century later in the 1977 Centenary Test on the same ground. Charles Bannerman scored the first Test century, retiring hurt on 165 after a ball split his finger. The two countries have played a Test series intermittently ever since.

The newspaper L'Auto was losing a circulation war with a rival sports daily when its editor Henri Desgrange approved a colleague's proposal: a multi-stage bicycle race around France, covered exclusively by L'Auto, to sell papers. Sixty riders started in July 1903; only twenty-one finished the six stages, some over 400 kilometres long and ridden through the night.

Maurice Garin, a chimney sweep turned professional cyclist, won by nearly three hours. Circulation of L'Auto roughly sextupled during the race. The event worked so well as publicity that Desgrange kept running it, and by the 1904 edition riders were already caught cheating by train and car.

The All England Croquet Club had a lawn going spare and a shortfall in its accounts, so in 1877 it added lawn tennis to its name and staged a gentlemen's singles tournament to raise funds for a pony roller. Twenty-two men entered, paying a guinea each.

Spencer Gore won the final in front of about two hundred spectators, and reportedly found the game repetitive to watch, predicting it would never catch on as a spectacle. Women's singles was not added until 1884. The scoring, court dimensions and rackets of that first tournament still shape the championship played today.

Only thirteen teams entered the first World Cup, and most of Europe stayed home rather than face a three-week sea crossing to Uruguay in the middle of the Depression. Uruguay had won Olympic football gold twice and built a new stadium, the Centenario, specifically to host the tournament.

Uruguay beat Argentina 4-2 in the final in front of a crowd reportedly over 90,000, having trailed at half-time. The trophy, later named after FIFA president Jules Rimet, was smuggled out of Italy inside a sock during the Second World War to keep it from Axis hands before being returned for the next tournament.

Baseball's National and American Leagues had been rivals rather than partners for two seasons when Boston's American League club and the National League's Pittsburgh Pirates agreed, on their own initiative, to a postseason series in 1903. No governing body ordered it; the leagues had not even fully reconciled their disputes.

Boston won five games to three in a best-of-nine format, behind pitcher Bill Dinneen's three victories. Cy Young pitched for Boston but lost his only decisive start. The next year's National League champion, John McGraw's New York Giants, refused to play a series at all, and the World Series did not become a fixed annual event until 1905.

Bobby Fischer forfeited game two of the 1972 Reykjavik match by refusing to appear over camera noise, putting him 2-0 down before a single move had counted, then won the title anyway, 12.5 to 8.5. He had also nearly abandoned the match before it started over prize money and playing conditions, and was talked back into it by phone calls from US officials who saw the contest as a Cold War prestige fight.

Spassky was the reigning champion and the Soviet chess establishment had dominated the title since 1948. Fischer became the first American to hold it, and the match drew far more mainstream press coverage than any chess event before or since. He never defended the title, forfeiting it in 1975 rather than play Anatoly Karpov under FIDE's terms, and largely vanished from public chess after.

Legend credits Go to the Emperor Yao, who supposedly designed it to teach discipline to a wayward son around 2300 BCE, but the earliest text to actually mention the game is the Zuo Zhuan, compiled centuries later and describing play around 548 BCE. Confucius later condemned idle men who wasted their days over it, an odd tribute to how established the game already was.

By around 500 BCE Go had settled into the form still played today: black and white stones placed on a grid, territory won by surrounding empty space rather than by capturing pieces outright. That single rule, simpler than chess and harder to master, is why the game spread through China, then Korea and Japan, largely unchanged for well over two thousand years.

Hnefatafl means kings table, and its board is deliberately unfair: one player commands a king and twelve defenders in the centre, the other twenty four attackers ringed around the edge. The defenders win by getting the king to any corner, the attackers by trapping him on all four sides, and it dominated Viking era boards from Iceland to Lapland for roughly nine hundred years.

No single medieval rulebook survives, so modern play is stitched together from regional variants that outlasted the game itself: Tablut recorded among the Sami, Brandubh in Ireland, Tawlbwrdd in Wales. All of them keep the same core imbalance, a lone king trying to outrun a numerically superior enemy, which is likely closer to what raiding and Viking politics actually felt like than any evenly matched game would.

Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator convinced that organised sport built character, convened a congress at the Sorbonne in June 1894 that he had partly disguised as a conference on amateurism to attract delegates. Representatives from twelve countries agreed to revive the ancient Games and formed the International Olympic Committee to run them.

Coubertin wanted the first modern Games held in Paris, but the Greek delegate Demetrios Vikelas argued for Athens as a symbolic home, and the committee agreed. Athens hosted the inaugural Games in 1896, with Coubertin serving as IOC president from 1896 to 1925.

On 15 April 1947 Jackie Robinson played first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field, going hitless but reaching base on an error and later scoring. No black player had appeared in the major leagues since the 1880s, when an informal owners agreement had shut them out. Branch Rickey, the Dodgers executive who signed him, had spent two years scouting Robinson specifically for his ability to take abuse without retaliating on the field.

Robinson had agreed, as a condition of the contract, not to answer taunts, brush-back pitches or spikes aimed at his legs. Teammates on the Dodgers threatened to strike rather than play with him; some were traded away instead. He won Rookie of the Year that season, and by the mid-1950s more than a dozen other black players had followed him into the majors.

Jesse Owens won the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and 4x100 metre relay at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, in front of a Nazi regime that had built the Games to promote claims of Aryan superiority. Hitler did not attend medal ceremonies for Black American athletes, though the widely repeated story that he stormed out specifically to snub Owens is not supported by contemporary accounts.

Owens returned home to segregation unchanged: no ticker-tape parade in his honour, and he was still barred from the front doors of some hotels that had celebrated him. Luz Long, the German long jumper he beat, publicly embraced him at the stadium and the two stayed in contact, a friendship the regime's own propaganda could not accommodate.

A group of wealthy racing enthusiasts began meeting in 1750 at the Star and Garter tavern on Pall Mall, forming a club that took its name from the jockeys and trainers whose sport it now governed from the owners' side of the table. There was no national rulebook for racing before this; disputes over weights, entries and match races had simply been settled locally, horse by horse.

Two years later the club leased land at Newmarket and built a coffee house there, giving it a permanent base in the town that was already the sport's unofficial capital. From Newmarket it set weights, licensed courses and adjudicated disputes across Britain, holding that authority for more than two and a half centuries until regulation passed to a separate body in 2006.

The pieces were real sheep or goat ankle bones, called astragaloi in Greek and tali in Latin, and the game around 800 BCE was closer to jacks than to dice. Players tossed a handful into the air and tried to catch as many as possible on the back of one hand, a skill game before it was ever a gambling one.

The same bones doubled as dice, each of the four sides given a different value, and as tools for telling fortunes, since a throw could be read for luck as easily as scored for a game. Children played it in the street and adults played it for stakes, and Greek vase paintings show both, sometimes in the same scene.

The earliest Roman mention of latrunculi comes not from a games manual but from Varro's book on the Latin language, written in the first century BCE, where he reaches for the game's grid as a comparison for grammar. The name means something close to the game of bandits, borrowed from a Greek predecessor called petteia that Homer's audience would already have recognised.

A poem called the Laus Pisonis describes a Roman senator drawing a crowd simply by playing a match, evidence the game carried real social weight rather than being a private amusement. Because so few sources describe the actual rules, historians still disagree over exactly how pieces captured one another, reconstructing play from board finds and passing literary references rather than any surviving rulebook.

Mary, Queen of Scots kept a billiard table during her long imprisonment in England, and complained by letter when her captors confiscated it. After her execution in 1587, her ladies wrapped her headless body in cloth taken from that same table, a detail recorded by an attendant at the scene and one of the odder survivals from her final years.

The game itself had already moved indoors from lawn versions played with a mallet and hoop, closer to croquet, onto a cloth covered table with raised edges. Wooden maces gradually gave way to the cue, and by the sixteenth century billiards was fashionable enough among European nobility that Shakespeare has a character in Antony and Cleopatra invite another to play.

A group of aristocratic cricketers broke away from an older White Conduit club and hired the bowler and groundsman Thomas Lord to find them a private ground, settling in 1787 on a field in Marylebone that gave the new club its name. Lord's original pitch stood elsewhere in London and moved twice before reaching its present St John's Wood site in 1814.

MCC soon took over writing and revising the laws of cricket, a role it held formally until 1993, and its members' distinctive red and yellow colours still mark cricket's most traditional ground. For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the club also picked England's touring teams, giving a private members' club unusual authority over an entire national sport.

Early tournaments were not the single lance charge people now picture but melees, mock battles between teams of knights fought across open country with real weapons and a real risk of death or capture. The one-on-one joust down a barrier, the version that survives in film, only became the centrepiece later, as armour and rules were refined to make the spectacle survivable.

Tournaments doubled as training for war and as a way for knights to win ransom money by capturing opponents rather than killing them, which gave the sport its own economy. Kings alternately banned and licensed them, worried that armed men gathering in numbers were as useful for rebellion as for sport, and church councils periodically condemned the practice as vainglorious and dangerous.

Mehen boards from around 3000 BCE take the shape of a coiled snake, its head carved at the centre and dozens, sometimes hundreds, of squares winding out to the tail. Sets came with small lion and lioness figures alongside marbles, and Egyptians clearly played it for centuries, since examples turn up across the Old Kingdom.

No ancient text explains how it worked, and no rulebook has ever surfaced, so Mehen is reconstructed purely from the boards and pieces themselves. The likeliest guess is a race game, marbles pushed along the spiral track towards the snake's head on throws of sticks or knucklebones, with the lion pieces perhaps used to capture an opponent along the way.

Rubber balls recovered from an Olmec sacrificial site at El Manati date to around 1600 BCE, the oldest worked rubber found anywhere, and the word Olmec itself comes from a Nahuatl term meaning rubber people. Players struck the heavy ball with hips, forearms or a padded yoke rather than hands or feet, keeping it off the ground through a game that could last hours.

Popular retellings make every match end in sacrifice, but the evidence points the other way: most games were ordinary contests, and only some ritual matches, tied to political or calendar occasions, ended with a captured player killed. The game spread from the Olmec across Mesoamerica and outlived them by two thousand years, still played by the Aztecs when the Spanish arrived.

The bull leaping fresco at Knossos, painted around 1450 to 1400 BCE, shows a leaper grasping the horns and vaulting clean over the animal's back, both men and women taking part. Unlike later bullfighting, nothing in Minoan art shows the bull being harmed, and it appears too often across seals, figurines and palace walls to be pure myth.

Most archaeologists now read it as sport and ritual at once, a genuinely dangerous test staged in a palace courtyard and then painted on the walls to advertise Knossos's power. Nobody has recovered rules or a written account of how it was scored or refereed, so everything known about the leap itself comes from how artists chose to freeze it.

The US ice hockey team at Lake Placid was mostly college players assembled months earlier, facing a Soviet squad that had won four straight Olympic golds and had just beaten an NHL all-star team 6-0. The US won 4-3 on 22 February 1980 after trailing twice, with Mike Eruzione scoring the winning goal midway through the third period. Al Michaels's closing question, whether anyone believed in miracles, became the game's shorthand.

It was not the gold medal game. The US still had to beat Finland two days later to win the tournament outright, which it did by coming back from a third-period deficit again. The Soviet team's coach, Viktor Tikhonov, was reportedly ordered by Soviet officials to bench his usual starting goaltender partway through the loss, a decision widely blamed at home for the defeat.

There was no pitch, no fixed number of players and often no ball rule beyond getting an inflated bladder to a marker at the far end of town, sometimes a church porch or a rival village's boundary stone. Games could involve hundreds of men and run for hours across fields, streets and rivers, with broken limbs common enough that some towns tried repeatedly to ban the practice.

Royal and civic authorities kept outlawing these matches, from Edward II's 1314 proclamation against football in London to later Tudor bans, mostly because the crowds disrupted trade and archery practice rather than out of concern for the players. A handful of English towns, including Ashbourne in Derbyshire, still hold an annual version of the game essentially unchanged.

For centuries the piece next to the king could only shuffle one square diagonally, making chess a slow game that could take an afternoon to open. Spanish and Italian sources from the late fifteenth century describe a faster variant in which that piece instead swept across the whole board in any direction, turning a plodding advisor into the strongest piece on the board.

The change, alongside giving the bishop its long diagonal range, produced something close to the game played today, and it spread through Italy and Spain within a few decades. Older, slower chess did not vanish overnight; the two versions coexisted in some regions for a generation before the faster queen became the standard everyone recognises now.

Parker Brothers first rejected the game pitched to them by Charles Darrow in 1934, citing fifty-two design flaws. Darrow had not invented it from scratch: he had learned a similar property-trading game, The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to illustrate the harms of monopolies, and reworked it with Atlantic City street names.

Parker Brothers relented after Darrow's home-made sets sold well on their own, and released Monopoly in 1935. Elizabeth Magie sold her original patent to the company for 500 dollars and no royalties, and Darrow was credited for decades as the game's sole inventor before her role became widely known.

Nadia Comaneci scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics on the uneven bars at Montreal on 18 July 1976, during the team compulsory competition. The scoreboard at the Forum had never been built to display a 10, since no one who designed it thought the score would ever be needed, so it flashed 1.00 instead while the crowd tried to work out what had happened.

She went on to score six more perfect 10s at those Games and won three gold medals at age fourteen, becoming the youngest Olympic gymnastics all-around champion at that point. Romania's state media made her a national symbol under Nicolae Ceausescu, though Comaneci later described her own training under coach Bela Karolyi as gruelling. She defected to the United States in 1989, months before Ceausescu's government fell.

Pankration entered the Olympic programme at the thirty third Games in 648 BCE, and its reputation for having no rules is not quite right. Only three moves were actually banned: biting, gouging an opponent's eyes and jamming a finger into his nose or mouth. Everything else, punches, kicks, chokes, joint locks and fighting on the ground, was fair.

Fighters competed bare handed and bare knuckled until someone submitted, was knocked out, or occasionally died in the ring, since a submission signalled by raising a finger came only when a competitor judged the alternative worse. One legendary victor, Arrhichion of Phigalia, is said to have won a final bout after already dying from a fatal hold, his opponent having tapped out moments earlier from a broken toe.

Patolli reaches back to around 200 BCE and spread far beyond the Aztecs, played by the Maya, Toltec, Zapotec and Mixtec as well, on a cross shaped board of fifty two spaces scratched into mats, floors or leather. Five drilled beans stood in for dice, and landing on a rival's piece sent it straight back to the start.

Colonial accounts describe stakes far past beans and counters: players wagered land, homes and, in the worst recorded cases, their own freedom. Spanish authorities banned the game in the sixteenth century as idolatry and burned the hands of people caught playing it, and it survived only in remote regions once the empire that gave it its biggest audience had fallen.

Pele was 17 when Brazil beat host Sweden 5-2 in the 1958 final in Stockholm, scoring twice and setting up a third with a chest-and-volley goal still replayed as one of the tournament's best. He had nearly missed the World Cup entirely after a knee injury kept him out of Brazil's early training, and only entered the squad for the third group match. He remains the youngest player to score in a World Cup final.

Brazil had never previously won the tournament, and the team wore an unfamiliar yellow shirt at this World Cup after their usual white kit was blamed for a traumatic 1950 final loss on home soil. Pele cried on the pitch after the final whistle and had to be consoled by teammate Gilmar. He went on to win two more World Cups, in 1962 and 1970.

Petteia turns up first not in a rulebook but in the Odyssey, where the suitors camped in Odysseus's palace pass the time playing it while they wait him out. By the fifth century BCE it was common enough that Plato and Aristotle both used it as a metaphor for skilled judgement, comparing a good statesman to a strong petteia player.

Pieces moved only in straight lines on a grid, commonly eight by eight, and a stone was captured by trapping it between two enemy pieces on opposite sides, never diagonally. Rome later borrowed the idea wholesale and renamed it latrunculi, meaning mercenaries or bandits, keeping the capture mechanic almost unchanged across several centuries and two languages.

The earliest record cited for playing cards is a single line in the Collection of Miscellanea at Duyang, written by the Tang author Su E, describing Princess Tongchang playing a leaf game with her husband's family in 868 CE. It is the oldest reference anyone can point to, not a description detailed enough to settle what the leaves actually looked like.

Scholars are genuinely split on whether yezi, the leaf game, meant cards at all in the ninth century or only came to mean that under the later Ming dynasty, centuries afterwards. Either way, printed cards with suits and ranks are firmly documented in China by the Song dynasty, and from there the idea travelled west along trade routes toward the decks Europe would adopt.

Music at Delphi predates any formal games, a contest tied to Apollo's shrine long before anyone counted years by Olympiads. What happened in 582 BCE was narrower: the festival was reorganised onto a four year cycle and athletics were added, foot races and chariot races borrowed straight from the Olympic model to sit alongside the older singing and lyre contests.

The Amphictyonic League, a council drawn from twelve Greek peoples, ran the festival and made a point of ranking music, drama and painting above sport, unlike the purely athletic Olympics. Winners left with a laurel wreath cut from the sacred grove rather than money, and the games kept running on the plain below Mount Parnassus for centuries after that reorganisation.

The Marquess of Queensberry did not write the rules that carry his name. A Welsh sportsman named John Graham Chambers drafted them in 1865, and Queensberry lent his title to their publication in 1867 to give the code social respectability, since bare-knuckle prizefighting was still widely treated as a criminal nuisance.

The twelve rules required padded gloves, introduced three-minute rounds with a minute of rest, and banned wrestling holds that London Prize Ring rules had allowed. A fighter knocked down had to rise unaided within ten seconds, the origin of the modern count. Amateur clubs adopted the code quickly; professional boxing followed by the 1890s.

Jeu de paume began as a courtyard game played with the bare palm, its French name literally meaning game of the palm, before players started wrapping their hands in gloves and then in webbed rackets. Monasteries provided some of the earliest playable courts, their cloisters offering the enclosed walls the game needed.

Sloped roofs, a lopsided net and openings called galleries all survive in real tennis courts today because they descend directly from the irregular architecture of those original enclosed spaces, not from a designed sport. The scoring by fifteens later carried straight over into lawn tennis, invented centuries afterward, which is why modern tennis still counts to game point in the same odd sequence.

Boards for the game turned up in the 1920s in graves at Ur dated to around 2600 BCE, twenty squares set out as a bird shaped path, inlaid with shell and lapis. For decades nobody knew how it was played, since the tombs held only the pieces, not the rules, and the game had died out long before anyone thought to write them down.

The answer came from a much later clay tablet the British Museum curator Irving Finkel decoded, written around 177 BCE by a Babylonian scribe. It described a race for two players moving seven pieces across the board on rolls of pyramidal dice, and matched the archaic layout closely enough that Finkel could confidently reconstruct a playable version of a game 2,400 years older than its own rulebook.

Erno Rubik, an architecture professor in Budapest, built his twisting cube in 1974 to help himself understand how independent parts could move without the whole structure falling apart, not as a toy. He called it the Magic Cube, and it took him about a month to solve his own invention the first time. Hungarian toy shops began selling small batches of it in 1977.

It only reached the wider world in 1980, when a Hungarian businessman and a British toy specialist licensed it to the Ideal Toy Corporation, which renamed it after its inventor. Over 100 million were sold in the following few years, and it is still the best-selling puzzle toy of all time. Rubik held onto the patent and later founded a studio in Budapest still producing puzzles and games.

An act of the Scottish parliament under James II ordered that futeball and golfe be utterly cryed doune, on the grounds that men were playing them instead of turning out for compulsory archery practice. England's longbow victories at Crecy and Agincourt still loomed large, and Scotland needed skilled archers against the same enemy.

The ban was reissued in 1471 and 1491, which is itself evidence it was not working: golf kept being played on the links land around St Andrews and elsewhere regardless of the law. Firearms eventually made archery obsolete for war, the prohibition lapsed unenforced, and golf's continued popularity on that same Scottish coastline is why the sport's home is usually traced there.

Alfred Butts, an unemployed architect during the Depression, had already spent years on an earlier tile game called Lexiko when he added a board in 1938, calling the result Criss-Crosswords. He worked out letter values by counting frequencies in the front page of the New York Times, which is why the Q and Z score high and the E does not.

Every major game company that saw it, including Parker Brothers and Milton Bradley, turned it down. Butts sold small runs himself for years until James Brunot bought the rights in 1948, simplified the rules, redesigned the board and renamed it Scrabble, the name under which it finally became a hit.

The oldest senet boards found in Egypt date to around 3100 BCE: thirty squares set in three rows, turned up in graves rather than houses. Early boards look like a plain race game, but by the New Kingdom scribes had linked the final squares to judgement and rebirth, so the pieces crossing the board stood for a soul crossing into the afterlife.

Tutankhamun was buried with four senet sets, and tomb paintings show the dead playing against an opponent nobody can see, a stand in for fate. No rulebook survives from any period, so every modern reconstruction of the throws and captures is pieced together from board layouts and scattered inscriptions, not from written instructions.

Klaus Teuber, an East German-trained dental technician turned game designer, published Die Siedler von Catan in Germany in 1995 through Kosmos, after years of designing games in his spare room. It won the Spiel des Jahres, Germany's top board game prize, within months, and its hexagonal tile board and resource-trading mechanics were unusual for a mass-market release at the time.

The game abandoned the elimination that dominated most board games then; players could be blocked but rarely knocked out entirely, and negotiation between players over trades became central to winning. Its success in Germany, and a slower English translation reaching wider audiences over the following decade, is widely credited with launching the modern hobby board game industry that followed.

Shogi grew out of chaturanga, the Indian game that also gave rise to chess, after it reached Japan by way of China and Korea. Its defining rule, that a captured piece changes sides and can be dropped back onto the board by its captor, has no equivalent in Western or Chinese chess and turns games into constant reversals of fortune.

The earliest physical evidence is a set of shogi pieces excavated at Kofukuji temple in Nara, dated to around 1058. The board settled at nine by nine squares only later; medieval variants used larger boards with extra piece types. The drop rule is what gives modern shogi its reputation as harder to draw than chess, since spare material never leaves the game.

Under the name Gyan Chaupar, or the knowledge game, players climbed a grid of squares each labelled with a virtue or a vice: generosity and faithfulness sent a token up a ladder toward liberation, while lust or theft dropped it down a snake's length back toward rebirth. The board was less a toy than a teaching tool, mapping karma and the soul's progress across a lifetime of choices.

British colonial administrators encountered the game in the nineteenth century and stripped out its moral vocabulary, keeping the ladders and snakes as pure mechanics and marketing it in Britain as Snakes and Ladders. Milton Bradley later sold the same skeleton in the United States as Chutes and Ladders, with slides replacing snakes, leaving the game's spiritual scoring system almost entirely forgotten.

Tabula replaced an older Roman race game, duodecim scriptorum, sometime in the first century CE, and kept its board of twenty four points with fifteen pieces a side moving anticlockwise on three dice. The clearest description of it comes not from a rulebook but from a poem mocking a real bad night at the table.

Around 480 CE the Byzantine emperor Zeno, playing white, threw a two, a five and a six that forced him to break up three safe pairs of pieces at once, exposing every one of them to capture. The poet Agathias wrote the throw up as proof that even an emperor could be ruined by dice, and it survives as the game's most detailed ancient account.

Fifteenth century Italian courts, including the Visconti and Sforza families of Milan, commissioned hand painted decks adding a fifth suit of 21 illustrated trump cards, plus the Fool, to the four ordinary suits already used for card games. The game played with them, tarocchi, was simply a trick taking game with extra permanent trumps, closer to modern bridge than to fortune telling.

Cartomancy using these same images did not appear until the late eighteenth century in France, roughly three hundred years after the decks were first painted for wealthy patrons in Italy. The occult meanings now attached to cards like the Hanged Man or the Tower were retrofitted long after the fact, onto artwork originally chosen for its resemblance to courtly pageants and allegorical processions.

Tiger Woods won the 1997 Masters at Augusta National by 12 strokes, the largest margin in the tournament's history, finishing at 18 under par, itself a Masters record at the time. He was 21 and had turned professional less than a year earlier. Augusta National had not admitted its first black member until 1990, and had barred black golfers from playing in the Masters at all until 1975.

Lee Elder, the first black golfer to play the Masters in 1975, watched from beside the first tee as Woods teed off in the final round, at Woods's own invitation. Woods wore a green jacket handed to him by the previous year's champion, Nick Faldo, and dedicated the win to his father, Earl, who had introduced him to golf as a toddler.

Chris Haney, a photo editor at the Montreal Gazette, and Scott Abbott, a Canadian Press sports editor, sketched out Trivial Pursuit on a kitchen table in December 1979 after discovering a Scrabble set missing pieces. It took them two more years to find manufacturers willing to fund it, and they sold shares in the game to friends and family to cover the costs.

Selchow and Righter licensed it for North America and it became the best-selling adult board game of the mid-1980s, with tens of millions of copies sold worldwide by 1984. Haney and Abbott had structured the game around six colour-coded categories after realising a single subject would bore most players, a format that most trivia games since have simply copied.

At the 2009 World Championships, Bolt covered the 100 metre distance in Berlin in 9.58 seconds, cutting more than a tenth of a second off his own previous world record from the Beijing Olympics the year before. His shoe had come untied during the Beijing final, where he slowed to celebrate before the line, prompting speculation about how much faster he might have run it out.

In Berlin he ran the full distance rather than easing up early, covering the 100 metres at 6 foot 5 with a stride length of over two and a half metres per step. Bolt also holds the 200 metres world record, set at the same 2009 championships. Both marks have stood for well over a decade since.

William Morgan ran the physical education programme at the Holyoke, Massachusetts YMCA and found that his older members found basketball, invented four years earlier just up the road, too rough. In 1895 he raised a tennis net and had two teams bat an inflated rubber bladder back and forth, calling the game Mintonette.

A colleague watching an early demonstration remarked on the volleying action and suggested the name volleyball instead, and it stuck. Morgan's original rules allowed unlimited players per side and no cap on how many times a team could touch the ball before returning it, both later tightened as the game spread through YMCAs worldwide.

Nintendo launched the Wii in North America in November 2006, built around a wand-like remote that read motion rather than the button-heavy controllers standard on rival consoles. It was less powerful than Sony's PlayStation 3 or Microsoft's Xbox 360, both released around the same time, and Nintendo deliberately sold it at a loss to undercut them on price rather than compete on graphics.

Wii Sports, bundled free with the console, introduced tennis, bowling and golf controlled by swinging the remote like a real racket or club, and sold hundreds of millions of copies as a result. It drew in older adults and non-gamers who had never bought a console before, and nursing homes began installing Wii bowling leagues, an audience Nintendo had not seriously targeted before.

Xiangqi shares an ancestor with Western chess but reads like a battlefield map rather than a courtly duel. Its river splits the board in two, cannons leap over other pieces to capture at a distance, and the general is confined to a small palace he can never leave, so the whole game is fought around protecting one nearly immobile piece.

The pieces, moves and the river-and-palace board reached their settled form during the Song dynasty, between the tenth and thirteenth centuries, after centuries of slower change from earlier Chinese board games. It remains the most played strategy game in China, and its cannon move, unknown in European chess, is usually credited to the era when gunpowder weapons were entering Chinese warfare.
